title: MCP 2026-07-28 Specification & Ecosystem Growth
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Core Maintainers shipped the **2026-07-28 specification** — the most significant revision to the protocol since its November 2024 launch. It reworks MCP's core transport model and adds a formal extensions framework, while remaining backward-compatible for servers that don't opt in to the new features.

---

## Stateless Core

The headline change: MCP shifted from a model where a client keeps a connection permanently open with a server, to one where **each request stands on its own** and carries all the information needed to handle it. Previously, session state (negotiated capabilities, subscriptions) lived in the long-lived connection itself, which meant a server process had to keep that connection pinned in memory.

Under the stateless core, requests can be **distributed across different server instances via a plain load balancer**, with no shared session storage required. This is a significant production win: MCP servers can now scale horizontally the same way a stateless REST API does, instead of needing sticky sessions or a shared session store.

---

## Other Protocol Changes

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can now span several request/response exchanges without holding a connection open the whole time.
- **Header-based routing** — requests carry routing metadata in headers rather than relying on connection-level context, which pairs naturally with the stateless core.
- **Cacheable list results** — `list_tools` / `list_resources`-style responses can now be marked cacheable, cutting redundant round-trips for clients (like Claude Code) that re-discover the same server's capabilities repeatedly.
- **Authorization hardening** — stronger OAuth and OIDC-based authorization flows, closing gaps in the original auth model that made enterprise deployments hesitant to expose sensitive MCP servers.
- **Formal extensions framework** — versioned extensions for *Apps* and *Tasks*, giving the spec a sanctioned way to grow new capability areas without breaking the core protocol.

---

## Claude Platform Support

Claude adopted the 2026-07-28 spec across its connector infrastructure. As of this update, Claude's connectors directory lists **over 950 MCP servers**, used by millions of people daily. New connector features tied to the spec update include embedded UI (a server can render interactive UI inside the client, not just return text/JSON), enterprise-managed authentication, observability hooks, and private network tunnels for connecting to internal-only servers.

---

## Adoption Numbers

Across MCP's Tier 1 SDKs, the protocol is seeing close to **half a billion downloads a month**. Individually, both the TypeScript and Python SDKs have each crossed **1 billion total downloads** — a rough proxy for how thoroughly MCP has become the default way agentic tools (including Claude Code) integrate with external systems, roughly 20 months after the spec's initial release.

---

## Governance Changes

The Core Maintainer group grew: **Clare Liguori** (AWS) joined as a Core Maintainer, and **Den Delimarsky** joined as a **Lead Maintainer**. On August 22, 2026, the Core Maintainers published an **updated roadmap** covering the next specification release and beyond, signaling MCP's governance is scaling alongside its adoption rather than staying a small, informal group.

---

## Why It Matters

The original MCP design (see the *Tool Use & Agents* page) prioritized a simple client-server plug that any agent could adopt. The 2026-07-28 spec keeps that simplicity for basic use cases but removes the two biggest blockers to running MCP servers in production at scale: statefulness (now optional-by-default rather than required) and weak authorization. For teams running Claude Code or other MCP clients against internal servers, this is the update that makes doing so a production-grade decision rather than a beta experiment.
